ART003062835.title: Computer Vision-based Basketball Player Training System

abstracts.value: Computer vision-based basketball player training system is a state-of-the-art field that relies on computer vision technologies and deep learning to help the basketball player train. Computer Vision-Based basketball player training systems rely on extensive training data to detect the player's movements and poses; the current training datasets are relatively small and vary in quality, affecting the basketball training effect. This paper proposes the human skeleton detection model, basketball and basketball hoop detection model, basketball shot detection model, basketball hit detection model, and basketball hit prediction model. In the proposed model, the basketball hit detection is improved by up to 9.66% over the existing method. The basketball hit prediction model is improved by up to 10.72% over the existing method using mathematical methods.

ART003267604.title: Computer simulation on the role of interproximal contacts in occlusal force transmission

abstracts.value: Purpose: This study aimed to investigate how interproximal contacts influence occlusal force transmission in the posterior maxilla using computer simulation. Materials and Methods: A three-dimensional model of the right maxillary second premolar, first molar, and second molar was constructed from patient CT data. Teeth and bone were defined as rigid bodies, and periodontal ligaments were represented by axial springs. Dynamic simulations were performed with occlusal forces of 100 N and 200 N applied at three points on the occlusal surface of the first molar for 0.1 s. Displacements of each tooth and the summed ligament forces were recorded and compared. Results: The first molar exhibited the greatest displacement and ligament forces, while the second premolar showed smaller secondary responses. Changes at the second molar were negligible. The peak displacement occurred on the mesial crown of the first molar, directed toward the second premolar. Increasing occlusal force from 100 N to 200 N markedly elevated the ligament forces at the first molar, whereas changes at the second premolar remained relatively small. These findings indicate that most additional load was dissipated locally at the first molar rather than transmitted distally, suggesting a limit in the load-sharing capacity of interproximal contacts. Conclusion: Occlusal forces applied to a single molar can be transmitted to adjacent teeth through interproximal contacts, and the extent depends on loading direction and contact geometry. Clinically, establishing proper proximal contacts is essential for controlled distribution of occlusal loads and the long-term stability of the dentition.
